Lee is a field operator kitted out for a long mission: a headset and bandana, a camo plate carrier loaded with pouches, a big rucksack with rope lashed to it, knee pads and worn boots. We built him to show how far we can push a realistic soldier for current-gen games.

Every piece of gear is its own believable object, with stitched webbing, scuffed buckles, dusty fabric and creased cargo pants that follow the body underneath. At 160K tris with five 4K and four 2K texture sets, the detail holds up in close-ups, and the beard and hair are an Alembic strand groom, so they move and catch light naturally. He's ready for gameplay or cinematic pipelines.

At Brothers Interactive, we contributed character cleanup, Sculpt & Texture Improvements, game res version and rigging services for multiple characters featured in The Midnight Walk, helping prepare scanned character assets for integration and use within the game pipeline.

T-Rex is our fan-art take on the Crash Bandicoot 4 look: a cartoon dinosaur with a huge grinning head, tiny arms, a spiky purple back and a long swinging tail. Crash 4 has one of the most recognizable stylized looks in games, so matching it was the whole point.

The sculpt pushes the shapes the way the game does, with chunky teeth, a squashed snout and simple, bold forms, and the textures carry all of it in a single 2K set with hand-tuned color. At 10K tris he's light enough for mobile and Switch while still holding up on PC and console. He shares a scene with our Beetle, and both were built to the same budget.

Need stylized creatures that match an established art style? This is the level we deliver.

SWAT V2 is the heavy unit of SWAT Squad, our own original set of tactical characters: a gas-mask helmet with round goggles, a full plate carrier, a backpack rig with cables and an antenna, and magazine and grenade pouches packed around the waist. He's the one you send through the door first.

All that gear has to stay readable, so the plate carrier, pouches, straps and webbing are built as separate layered pieces with real thickness, and yellow trim lines guide the eye across the silhouette. Up close you get worn fabric, scuffed boots and stitched straps at 4K texture density. He's fully rigged and tested with production motion data, and the red version shows his texture variants.

Tiger is the lead of The Last Rebel (TLR), our own original universe. As the hero, he had to carry the whole look of the project: a battle-worn tiger warrior in heavy plate, with glowing runes on the armor, bloodied wraps and a torn red sash.

The sculpt balances animal anatomy with armor that still lets him move, with plates broken up around the shoulders, elbows and knees, and fur, steel, leather and cloth that each read clearly in engine. Zombie-2 has been dead a lot longer: a gaunt, leathery body with skin shrunk tight over the bones, an open torso, white hair still tied back in a bun, and the cargo pants and boots of whoever this used to be. Where Zombie-1 is fresh, this one is dried out, and together they show the range a horde needs.

At 120K tris there's room for the hard parts: tendons and ribs pushing through dry skin, exposed tissue in the stomach, and hair cards for the long white hair. The same texture setup as Zombie-1 (four 4K, two 2K and one 1K sets) carries the cracked skin and stained fabric, and the high-to-low bake keeps the fine detail at game resolution.

Zombie-1 is a freshly turned walker: a torn shirt, rotting skin, a jaw pulled back over broken teeth, and thinning hair still hanging on. He's built to be the face of a horde, readable from across a street and still nasty in a close-up.

The sculpt layers the decay in passes, from the overall body to wounds, peeling skin and swollen tissue, then bakes it all down to an 80K-tri game mesh. Four 4K, two 2K and one 1K texture sets handle the blood, grime and wet tissue, and the jeans and boots get their own wear, so the clothes never look cleaner than the man. He's shown in Unreal Engine, ready for gameplay and cutscenes.

Murkaz comes from Man to God (MTG), our own original universe drawn from Indian mythology. We built him as a boss-sized brute: heavy frame, braided beard, fur everywhere, and a mace big enough to sell every hit, made to carry a boss fight in gameplay and still hold the camera in a cutscene.

The sculpt does the heavy lifting, with real weight in the belly, shoulders and calves, and leather, cloth and metal that each read differently. The lion-head pauldron, carved mace, face paint and embroidered cloth carry most of the surface detail.

items.desc:
We made CHR Skins to show what a cosmetics pipeline looks like when it's built for volume. Every outfit is a set of swappable pieces (top, layer, jeans, shoes) on one shared base body, so new skins come from recombining and retexturing, not rebuilding.

Five base sets (hoodie, shirt, leather jacket, denim jacket and sleeveless denim vest) become 15 distinct looks through color, wash and wear passes. Swap the tops, bottoms and shoes between them and you get hundreds of casual outfits, with fabric that reads as real fleece, cotton and denim at gameplay distance. Topology stays consistent across pieces, so skin weights carry over and everything mixes and matches without clipping.

Need a steady stream of skins for a multiplayer, live-service or streetwear-style game? This is how we'd build it.

items.t: Sir Galahad: The Order 1886 Fan Art
items.desc:
Sir Galahad is our take on the lead knight from The Order: 1886, built from scratch to match a AAA cinematic look. The goal was simple: could our version hold up in the same kind of close-up shots as the original?

The uniform does most of the talking: a wool coat with gold braiding, a leather belt rig with holster and dagger, an embroidered cape emblem, and engraved steel bracers and greaves, each with its own wear and edge breakup. The face and beard are sculpted for close-ups, and the coat and cape are built as clean quad meshes, ready for rigging and cloth sim.

Planning a story-driven action game with period costume? Talk to us about your hero.

items.desc:
Adam is a five-stage progression character: one stylized boy who grows from a schoolkid into a fully armored warrior. Each stage adds gear on top of the last, so the player sees the journey on the model itself.

Stage 1 is the base schoolboy, stage 2 adds a rebel's mask, vest and pouches, stage 3 a bow and quiver, stage 4 a sword and light armor, and stage 5 the full knight set with crested helmet, cape and shield. Everything sits on one base body and skeleton, so gear attaches and swaps cleanly. The budget stays low and texturing starts from a single 2K map, so the full set runs on mobile and Switch as well as PC.

Planning an RPG or progression game with visible character upgrades? Talk to us about your hero.

items.desc:
Explorer's Book (first made as our Proposal Book) came out of a 12-week masterclass our team took on the game prop pipeline. It's an explorer's kit packed onto one book: a green embossed leather journal strapped shut, a rolled bamboo mat, a spyglass, a quill and pencil, wax-sealed letters, coins, dice and loose sketch pages.

The challenge was making a pile of small objects read as one prop. Leather, paper, bamboo, brass and glass each get their own wear, and the loose pages and straps are arranged so the silhouette works from any angle. It's built to be seen up close, on a desk, in an inspect view or in a story moment.

Need props that tell a story up close? Talk to us about your project.

items.desc:
Fire Drum is a hand-pumped coal furnace: a dented red drum stove full of glowing coals, a wooden bellows feeding air through a wrapped cloth hose, and a pan of coal beside a stack of metal plates. It's the sort of working prop that makes a blacksmith's corner, a street vendor or a survival camp feel lived in.

Every surface shows how it's been used: chipped paint and rust on the drum, scorch marks around the air holes, soot on the plates, and frayed, dusty fabric on the hose. It sits at 14K tris with three 2K texture sets (drum, coals and bellows), and the coals are set up for emissive glow and particles in engine.

Need props that make a scene feel used and believable? Talk to us about your environment.

items.desc:
Our fan-art take on the Pip-Boy 2000 from the Fallout series: the chunky wrist computer with a green CRT screen, dials, a speaker grille and a padded red cuff. A prop like this sits right in front of the first-person camera, so every surface gets looked at.

We kept the retro-industrial feel, with olive paint chipped down to the metal, hazard stripes, warning stickers, worn leather straps and a scratched glass screen. Even with all that detail it's only 8K tris on a single 2K texture set, with clean topology and pivots on the moving parts, so the screen and controls can be animated and the display can show live UI in engine.

items.desc:
Dhakad is a portrait study of a hardened old warrior-sage: a bald head, deep wrinkles, a scar across the cheek, sacred ash and tilak marks on the forehead, and a long grey beard. The goal was a face that tells his whole story before he says a word.

The sculpt sets the big forms first, then the wrinkles, pores and scar tissue that sell his age. The beard starts as a sculpted shape for planning, then becomes hair cards for the final: 17K tris of hair on a 25K-tri head, with a 4K map for the head and a 2K map for the hair. The facial topology is laid out for blendshapes and dialogue close-ups.

Need a memorable face for a story-driven game? Talk to us about your characters.

items.desc:
Head Study - Benedict Wong

Developed internally at Brothers Interactive, "Head Study" represents our team's foundational strength in hyper-realistic organic sculpting and secondary form definition. This high-poly asset was developed to showcase an advanced understanding of facial fat distribution, complex skin micro-detailing, and natural tissue weight distribution required for high-fidelity AAA character generation.

Rasch is our fan-art take on Karl Ernst Rasch from Crysis 3, the veteran who helps the resistance from behind the scenes. Instead of armor and weapons, the challenge here was an ordinary older man who still had to feel at home in a AAA shooter.

The likeness carries it: grey hair, glasses, and wrinkles and skin that sag naturally with age. His field gear is worn but practical, with a canvas shirt, a padded vest carrying a radio and devices, and cargo pants with reinforced knees, each with its own wear and fabric detail. The wireframes show tidy, game-ready topology with extra loops around the face for expression.

Working on a story-heavy game with supporting characters who need to feel real? Talk to us about your cast.
